With three days left in Epoch 1 of the @termix_ai × Kaito campaign, one topic deserves more attention: dispute resolution.

The process has four stages. Funds are locked, proof of completion is submitted, and if a dispute occurs, three randomly selected evaluators step in. The team cannot overturn a decision simply because it disagrees with the outcome.

That matters in a system where AI agents hire and pay each other. Trust depends on the same rules being applied to everyone.

But the difficult question remains: what happens if all three evaluators reach the wrong decision?

Removing team intervention can make the system more transparent, but clear rules alone do not create trust. What matters is how the protocol responds when those rules produce a bad outcome.

You can publish 10 posts per epoch, but only your best 6 count. Across the full campaign, the final score comes from your top 18 posts. With 450 creators earning rewards and $TMT allocations unlocking 100% at TGE, this is the time to focus on questions that actually matter.

For @termix_ai, the real test may begin when the dispute system gets something wrong.

2110084887730417679.author: doodlestein
2110084887730417679.tweetText:
When Michael Crichton (the author of Jurassic Park and many other great novels) was in college at Harvard, he had a writing professor who didn’t like him or his work and kept criticizing it and giving him bad grades.

He decided to demonstrate that the prof had it in for him by submitting an essay by George Orwell instead. Of course, the professor gave it a B-. See pics for details.

I’m totally convinced that the rabid hordes of AI-hating programmers frothing at the mouth about “vibe coded slop” would similarly be dismissive of perfectly crafted code by Fabrice Bellard or John Carmack if it were taken out of context and they suspected it was produced with help from AI agents.

These people don’t actually know what good code looks like. They’re often too incompetent and unlettered to even understand the purpose and nature of various algorithms and systems (for instance, the cancel-correct structured concurrency primitives that I use across all my projects from asupersync) and why they’re useful and better. 

Why would they? This is often hard stuff that was relegated to academic CS journals and dissertations just a few years ago, and these people are, by and large, complete imbeciles. 

Anyway, just keep that in mind next time you see the people showing up in numbers (always with utterly unimpressive GitHub profiles with 3 forks and a trivial project or two) to declare my work as “slop” and dismiss me for having “AI psychosis.”

I would say to pity them for the fact that economic reality is about to slam into them like a brick wall, except many of them are so antisocial and nasty that they deserve that wake-up call and reality check.
